main.claim: Open the dictation practice in your browser, press play, and type the sentence you hear. Check marks each word green if it is right and red if it is wrong or missing, with an accuracy score and a running session score.

sections.heading: How English dictation practice works
sections.body:
Dictation is a simple loop: you hear a sentence, you write it down, and you check what you got wrong. This tool runs that loop in your browser.

1. Open [English dictation practice](https://dictation-practice.lazur.app/).
2. Pick easy, medium or hard.
3. Press play. The browser reads one English sentence aloud.
4. Type exactly what you hear.
5. Press Check and read the result before you move on.

**Type what you hear, not what you expect.** If you miss a short word, type your best guess, check it, and look at the red word. The mistakes you find are the ones worth practicing.

sections.heading: Pick a level and control the speed
sections.body:
There are three levels: easy, medium and hard. Start with easy if the sentences blur together. Move up when the words feel clear and most of your words turn green.

Use the speed slider to change how fast the browser reads. Replay plays the sentence again at the speed you chose. Slow replay plays it more slowly, which helps when one word goes by too fast. Use slow replay to catch the word you missed, then replay at normal speed to hear it inside the full sentence.

Do not replay a sentence until you can copy it. Listen first, type, and replay only when you need to catch a word. The goal is to hear the sentence as well as you can the first time.

sections.heading: What the Check result tells you
sections.body:
Press Check after you type. Each correct word turns green. Each wrong or missing word turns red. The accuracy score shows how much of the sentence you got right, and the running session score adds up across the sentences you finish.

**Read the red words first.** A red word can mean a spelling mistake, a word you did not hear, or a word you left out. Replay the sentence and listen for that one word. Type the sentence again, then press Check once more to see the change.

sections.heading: Why dictation builds listening and spelling
sections.body:
When you write a sentence from sound alone, you have to decide every word. That makes you notice small words such as a, the and to, and endings such as the s on a plural or the ed on a past verb. Those are easy to skip when you only follow the meaning.

Writing from sound also shows you how English spelling works for words you already know by ear. A word that sounds the same as another can be spelled two ways, and Check will show you which one you chose.

Short, regular practice works better than one long session. Ten minutes a day gives you more chances to hear the same sounds than one hour a week.

sections.heading: Practice every day
sections.body:
Pick one level and stay with it for a few days. Note the words that turn red most often, then listen for them in the next session. When the same word stops turning red, move to a harder sentence.

If you dictate every day, Lazur does this in any app on your Mac. Hold two keys and talk, and it types into whatever app you are in, at [lazur.app](https://www.lazur.app).

pages.title: English Dictation Practice for Beginners: Easy Level | Lazur
pages.description: Start English dictation at the easy level. The browser reads each sentence aloud, you type it, and Check marks every word green or red so you see what to fix.
pages.claim: Choose easy, press play, and type each sentence the browser reads aloud. Check marks each word green or red, so you see which words you missed. Use slow replay whenever a sentence blurs together.

sections.heading: Start at the easy level
sections.body:
Open the [beginner dictation page](https://dictation-practice.lazur.app/beginners) and follow these steps for your first session.

1. Choose easy.
2. Press play and listen once without typing.
3. Type the sentence you hear, word by word.
4. Press Check and read the green and red words.

Beginners often type the sentence they expect to hear. Type what you actually hear instead. If you are unsure of a word, type your best guess. Check will show you the right one, and that one correction is worth more than a sentence you copied from memory.

sections.heading: Use the speed and replay controls
sections.body:
The speed slider changes how fast the browser reads. Start with a speed you can follow without strain. Replay plays the sentence again at that speed, and slow replay plays it at a lower speed so you can pick out each word.

Use slow replay only when a word is lost. If you need it for every sentence, lower the speed slider a little and keep listening. Then try normal replay once, so your ear gets used to the pace of real English speech.

You do not need to finish every sentence in one go. Stop after a few sentences, read your session score, and come back the next day. Short sessions help you keep your attention on the sounds.

sections.heading: What the green and red words mean
sections.body:
Each word you typed right turns green. Each word that is wrong or missing turns red. A red word does not mean you failed the sentence. It shows you exactly where your ear and your spelling need work.

The accuracy score shows how much of the sentence you got right. The running session score adds up as you finish sentences, so you can see progress across a session without counting by hand.

**Start with the first red word.** Replay the sentence and listen for that word only. Type the sentence again and press Check. When that word turns green, move on to the next red one.

sections.heading: The small words beginners miss
sections.body:
The most common red words in beginner sentences are small ones: a, the, to, is, and the endings on verbs and nouns. English speakers often say these quickly and softly, so they are easy to miss even when the rest of the sentence is clear.

Endings are the next most common miss. A plural s and a past tense ed are often very short. Listen for the sound at the end of the word, not only the start, and type the ending even when it seems quiet.

If the red words are always small ones, that is a sign to slow down, not to give up. Use slow replay once, then listen to the whole sentence again at normal speed. The rhythm of the sentence will help you place the small word.

sections.heading: When to move up to medium
sections.body:
Move to medium when most of your words turn green on easy and you no longer need slow replay for most sentences. A session where the accuracy score stays high across several sentences is a good sign.

Do not rush the move. If you jump up too early, the sentences will feel fast and the red words will pile up. You can always go back to easy for a day when you want a confidence boost, then return to medium the next day.

faq.q: How do beginners practice English dictation?
faq.a: Choose the easy level, press play, and listen once. Type the sentence you hear, then press Check. Read the green and red words, replay the sentence if you need to, and try the next one. Ten minutes a day is enough to start.

faq.q: Which level should a beginner choose?
faq.a: Start with easy. It is built for people who are still learning to catch English words by ear. Move to medium once most of your words turn green and you no longer need slow replay for most sentences.

Usually the sentence came through too fast to catch, or you typed the words in a different order than you heard them. Use slow replay, listen again, and type one word at a time. Then press Check again to see the change.

pages.title: English Dictation Practice for Kids: Listen and Type | Lazur
pages.description: Let a child practice English dictation in the browser. The sentence is read aloud, they type it, and Check shows each right and wrong word. Easy level to start.
pages.claim: Choose easy, press play, and have your child type what they hear. Check shows right words in green and wrong or missing words in red straight away. The slow replay helps when a sentence goes by too fast.

sections.heading: How to start with a child
sections.body:
This tool is an English dictation page for anyone who can read and type, so an adult or older child may need to help a younger one get started. Sit with them for the first session and read the steps together.

1. Open the [dictation practice for kids](https://dictation-practice.lazur.app/kids) in a browser.
2. Choose easy.
3. Press play and ask the child to listen once.
4. Ask them to type what they heard, then press Check.

For a young child, say the steps out loud before each sentence. The goal of the first session is to see the green and red words together and understand what they mean, not to finish a set number of sentences.

sections.heading: Use replay without making it a guessing game
sections.body:
Replay and slow replay are there to help a child catch a word they missed. Use them once per sentence. If a child presses replay again and again and types whatever comes to mind, the practice stops working, because they are guessing instead of listening.

The speed slider can make the sentences easier to follow. Lower it a little for a child who is still getting used to English sounds. Raise it back toward normal speed once the sentences start to feel comfortable.

sections.heading: Read the result together
sections.body:
When Check shows red words, talk about them with the child. Ask what they heard. Often the child heard a sound but did not know the spelling, or they heard a word that was not in the sentence. Both are useful things to notice.

Green words are worth praising too. A child who gets most of a sentence right needs to know that the work is paying off. The accuracy score and the session score give a simple number to talk about, but the words themselves matter more than the number.

sections.heading: Keep sessions short
sections.body:
Children learn best in short, regular sessions. Five to ten minutes a day is a good target. Stop before the child gets tired, and end on a sentence they got right. That leaves them with a good feeling about English and makes them more willing to come back.

If the easy level feels too hard after a few sessions, look at the speed first, then the level. If it feels too easy, move to medium when the child is ready.

Parents and teachers can sit beside the child for the first week and then step back. Let the child press play and type on their own, and help only when the same red word shows up more than once. That slow handover builds independence without leaving the child to struggle alone.

faq.q: Can kids practice English dictation online?
faq.a: Yes. Open the page in a web browser, choose easy, and press play. The browser reads a sentence aloud and the child types it. Check then marks each word green or red, so the child can see exactly what to fix.

faq.q: What level should a child start on?
faq.a: Start with easy. Listen to the first few sentences together, then check the Check result. If most words turn green, the child can try medium. If the words are mostly red, keep easy and use slow replay for the hard words.

faq.q: How long should a child practice dictation each day?
faq.a: Five to ten minutes is a good target for most children. Short sessions keep attention on the sounds. Stop while the child still wants to continue, and end on a sentence they got right.

pages.title: English Dictation Practice for Students: Build Accuracy | Lazur
pages.description: Use English dictation to sharpen listening and spelling. Students hear a sentence, type it, and get Check results with an accuracy score. Three levels.
pages.claim: Open the dictation, pick easy, medium or hard, and type each sentence you hear. Check marks wrong and missing words in red and shows an accuracy score and a running session score, so you can track your work.

sections.heading: A study routine that uses dictation
sections.body:
Dictation fits well into a study session because it needs only your ears, a keyboard and a few minutes. Use it before a listening class, a language exam or a writing task, when you want your ear and your spelling to be ready.

1. Open the [student dictation practice](https://dictation-practice.lazur.app/students).
2. Pick the level that matches your class.
3. Work through a set of sentences, typing each one before you check.
4. Press Check after each sentence and note the red words.

Keep a short list of the words that gave you trouble. Review that list at the start of your next session, before you open a new set of sentences.

It also helps to set one small goal per session, such as getting every red word in one sentence to green. A clear goal keeps the practice focused, and you will know when the session is done.

sections.heading: Choose the right level
sections.body:
Easy, medium and hard are the three levels. If you are new to English dictation, start with easy and build your confidence. If you already follow most spoken English, medium or hard will give you more to work on.

The speed slider lets you slow the browser down or speed it up. Use normal speed as your target. Lower the speed only for the sentences that you cannot follow, then return to normal speed on the next pass.

sections.heading: Use the scores to track your work
sections.body:
The accuracy score shows how much of the current sentence you got right. The running session score adds up as you finish sentences. Together they give you a quick way to see whether your work is improving during a session.

**Do not chase a perfect score on your first try.** A low score on a hard sentence can teach you more than a high score on an easy one. Look at the red words, replay the sentence, and try the same sentence again. Watch which words change from red to green.

sections.heading: Spelling and listening together
sections.body:
Most students know more words than they can hear clearly in a fast sentence. Dictation shows both problems at once. A red word can mean you did not hear the sound, or you heard it but did not know how to spell it.

To tell which one it is, replay the sentence and listen to that word alone. If you cannot hear it even slowly, the problem is listening. If you hear it clearly and still type the wrong letters, the problem is spelling, and a short note in your notebook can help you remember it.

Keep the notebook page simple: the word, the sentence it came from, and one sentence about why you missed it. When you review the notebook a week later, you will see which kinds of mistakes repeat, and you can practice exactly those.

faq.q: How do students use English dictation practice?
faq.a: Open the page, pick a level, and type each sentence before you press Check. Note the red words, replay the sentence to hear them, and review your list of tricky words at the start of your next session.

faq.q: What does the accuracy score mean?
faq.a: The accuracy score shows how much of the current sentence you typed correctly. Correct words turn green and wrong or missing words turn red. Use the red words to decide what to practice next.

faq.q: Can dictation help with a language exam?
faq.a: It can help with listening and spelling, which are part of many English tests. This tool uses general English sentences at three levels. It does not copy any exam, so pair it with the practice materials your exam provides.

pages.title: English Dictation Practice for Class 6: Levels and Tips | Lazur
pages.description: This dictation tool is not built for a Class 6 syllabus. It has easy, medium and hard English sentences to practice listening and spelling. Here is how to use it.
pages.claim: This tool does not follow a Class 6 syllabus or a school word list. It has easy, medium and hard sentences. Type what the browser reads aloud, and Check marks each word, so a Class 6 student can practice the same skill.

sections.heading: What this tool covers for Class 6
sections.body:
This page does not follow a Class 6 syllabus, and it does not use a set list of words from any school or board. It reads general English sentences at three levels: easy, medium and hard. For a student in Class 6, the practice is the same skill their teacher checks in dictation: hearing each word and writing it correctly.

If your teacher gives you a dictation passage, use this tool for extra practice on the same skill. Use the level that matches how fast your class reads the passage, then move to the next level when your work gets easier.

If you are not sure which level fits, try one sentence on each level and compare how many words turn red. Choose the level where you get most words right but still see a few red ones. That is the level where you learn the most.

sections.heading: Steps for a Class 6 session
sections.body:
1. Open the [Class 6 dictation practice](https://dictation-practice.lazur.app/class-6).
2. Pick the level that matches your classwork.
3. Press play and listen to the whole sentence once.
4. Type what you hear, then press Check.
5. Read the red words and replay the sentence to hear each one.

Keep a short list of the words you miss, including small words such as the, a and to, and endings such as s and ed. Review the list before your next session.

If you have a class test coming up, use the same levels in the days before it. Start each session with the sentences you missed last time, then move to new ones. Doing the same kinds of sentences several days in a row helps you hear the patterns your teacher is likely to use.

sections.heading: Use the speed controls
sections.body:
The speed slider changes how fast the browser reads each sentence. Replay plays it again at the speed you set. Slow replay plays it more slowly, which helps when one word is hard to catch.

Use slow replay for the one word you missed, then listen at normal speed so you hear it inside the full sentence. Students who replay a sentence many times without typing often end up guessing, so type first and replay only when you need to.

sections.heading: Track progress across a session
sections.body:
The accuracy score shows how much of each sentence you got right. The running session score adds up as you finish sentences, so you can see whether a session is going well.

**Look for words that stay red.** A word that turns red again and again is the one to practice. Write it down, listen to it alone, then type the sentence once more. When that word turns green, you have learned it for this session.

faq.q: Does this dictation tool follow the Class 6 syllabus?
faq.a: No. The tool does not use a Class 6 syllabus or a school word list. It offers general English sentences at easy, medium and hard levels. It can help a Class 6 student practice listening and spelling, but it does not replace a teacher's dictation work.

faq.q: Which level should a Class 6 student choose?
faq.a: Choose the level that matches how fast your classwork is read to you. If most words turn green, move up. If many words stay red even with slow replay, stay on the easier level and practice a few sentences each day.

faq.q: How can a Class 6 student practice dictation at home?
faq.a: Open the page, choose a level, and type each sentence before pressing Check. Review the red words, replay the sentence to hear them, and keep a short list of tricky words to review at the start of the next session.

pages.title: English Spelling Practice for Kids: Type and Check | Lazur
pages.description: Practice English spelling with kids in the browser. The sentence is read aloud, they type it, and Check marks each misspelled word in red right away.
pages.claim: Choose easy, press play, and type the sentence the browser reads aloud. Check marks each misspelled or missing word in red and each correct word in green, so your child sees each spelling mistake right away.

sections.heading: Spelling inside sentences
sections.body:
This page practices spelling inside full English sentences rather than in a list of single words. The browser reads a sentence aloud, your child types what they hear, and Check shows which words are right. A word that is spelled wrong turns red, so the mistake is easy to see. Green words show the spellings that are already right, so your child can see what they are doing well as well as what to fix.

Sentences help with spelling because words appear in context. A child who writes the word in a sentence has to hear the sound, choose the letters and keep the rest of the sentence in order.

sections.heading: How to run a spelling session
sections.body:
1. Open the [spelling practice for kids](https://dictation-practice.lazur.app/spelling-kids).
2. Choose easy to start.
3. Press play and have your child listen once.
4. Ask them to type the sentence, spelling each word as they go.
5. Press Check and look at the red words together.

For each red word, replay the sentence, listen for that word, and type it again. Then press Check once more. The word has to turn green before the child moves on.

sections.heading: Use replay for hard spellings
sections.body:
The speed slider changes how fast the sentence is read. Replay plays it again, and slow replay plays it more slowly. Use slow replay for a word the child cannot catch, then listen at normal speed to hear it in the sentence.

Do not let replay turn into guessing. Ask the child to type the sentence once before they replay it, so the practice stays focused on listening and spelling.

If the same word keeps turning red across several days, write it on a card with the sentence it came from. Read the card together before the next session. Seeing the word written out often helps more than hearing it again and again.

sections.heading: Keep it short and encouraging
sections.body:
Spelling practice works best in short sessions. Five to ten minutes a day is enough for most children. Stop while they still want to keep going, and finish on a sentence they spelled correctly.

A good way to end is to replay the last sentence they got right and ask them to type it once more with no help. Seeing a full sentence come out correct is a clear sign of progress, and it gives them something to build on the next day.

When red words appear, talk about the spelling rather than the mistake. Ask which letters the child chose and why. Many spelling errors come from a sound that can be written more than one way, and naming that pattern helps a child remember it next time.

faq.q: How can kids practice English spelling online?
faq.a: Open the page in a web browser, choose easy, and press play. The browser reads a sentence aloud, and the child types it. Check marks each misspelled word in red, so the child can see which spellings to fix.

faq.q: Does this practice use word lists?
faq.a: No. The practice uses English sentences at three levels, so spelling is practiced in context. Words appear inside sentences, which helps a child hear the sound and choose the right letters.

faq.q: How often should a child practice spelling?
faq.a: Short sessions of five to ten minutes a day work well for most children. Regular practice helps more than one long session each week. Stop while the child is still interested and end on a sentence they spelled correctly.

pages.title: English Spelling Practice for Adults: Dictation Method | Lazur
pages.description: Practice English spelling as an adult with dictation. Type each sentence you hear, and Check marks misspelled and missing words in red. Three levels in your browser.
pages.claim: Practice spelling by typing English sentences you hear. Check shows each correct word in green and each misspelled or missing word in red, with an accuracy score and a running session score.

sections.heading: Why spelling practice works best in sentences
sections.body:
Many adults know a word when they see it but hesitate when they have to write it. Dictation fixes that gap, because you hear the word and then write it yourself. The practice in this tool uses full English sentences at easy, medium and hard levels, so spelling is practiced in context.

A sentence also shows you how words fit together. When a word is spelled wrong, the rest of the sentence still gives you clues about meaning, which helps you remember the right form.

sections.heading: Run a spelling session
sections.body:
1. Open the [adult spelling practice](https://dictation-practice.lazur.app/spelling-adults).
2. Choose the level that matches your confidence.
3. Press play and listen to the whole sentence once.
4. Type the sentence exactly as you heard it.
5. Press Check and read the red words.

For each red word, replay the sentence, listen for that word, and type it again. Press Check once more to confirm the change. A word that turns green has been fixed for this session.

sections.heading: Read the accuracy score
sections.body:
The accuracy score shows how much of the current sentence you typed correctly. The running session score adds up as you finish sentences. Use them to see where you stand, but read the red words first, because they show what to work on.

A red word can be a spelling error, a word you did not hear, or a word you left out. Replay the sentence to find out which. If you hear the word clearly and still spell it wrong, write the correct form in a notebook and type the sentence again later in the session.

sections.heading: Spelling patterns that catch adults
sections.body:
Many English spelling errors come from sounds that can be written more than one way, such as the vowel in words with ei and ie, or the endings that sound alike but are spelled differently. Words that sound the same but have different meanings are another common source of errors.

When a red word shows one of these patterns, slow down and think about the spelling before you type. Then repeat the sentence later in the same session. Repetition across a session helps the spelling stay with you longer than one quick check.

Adults who practice at work or during a course often have only a few minutes at a time. That is enough. Do one short set of sentences, note the red words, and come back to them the next time you sit down. A steady habit of a few sentences will do more for your spelling than an occasional long session that you do not finish.

faq.q: How can an adult practice English spelling?
faq.a: Open the page, choose a level, and listen to a sentence once. Type it exactly as you heard it, then press Check. Replay the sentence for each red word, type it again, and watch the words turn green.

faq.q: What do the green and red words mean?
faq.a: Green means the word is correct. Red means the word is misspelled, missing or wrong. The red words show you exactly what to practice in the next sentence or session.

faq.q: Is dictation a good way to improve spelling?
faq.a: Dictation makes you choose every letter from sound, which trains spelling and listening together. This tool gives you that practice at three levels, with an accuracy score so you can see your work across a session.
